The Antarctic toothfish Dissostichus mawsoni exhibits several life-history traits shaped by the frigid, stable conditions of the Southern Ocean. Incubating eggs at near-freezing temperatures of 0 °C [T = 0 °C] results in a protracted embryonic development, with hatching occurring after 75 days [ab = 75 days], a duration that aligns with the slow metabolic pace typical of polar teleosts. At the moment of chorion rupture, the emerging yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.0477 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0477 grams], a diminutive starting mass derived from a small egg diameter. This lecithotrophic phase persists until the yolk sac is fully resorbed and the mouth is open, after which the first exogenous feeding begins. The ultimate total length attained by this species reaches 200 centimeters [Li = 200 centimeters], based on captures of very large adults in the Ross Sea region, making it one of the largest nototheniids.

Puberty in Dissostichus mawsoni is reached after a considerable period of somatic growth, with individuals becoming sexually mature at a body length of 133.2 centimeters [Lp = 133.2 centimeters]. The time since birth at the onset of puberty spans approximately 2,920 days [tp = approximately 2,920 days] when fish experience the typical bottom water temperature of 1.3 °C [T = 1.3 °C], which corresponds to roughly eight years of age. This extended juvenile phase is consistent with the slow life-history pace of high-latitude fishes, where cold temperatures depress metabolic and developmental rates. During this period, the fish accumulate substantial lipid reserves in their musculature, a necessary adaptation for enduring the seasonal scarcity of prey. The length at which maturity occurs also shows some variability across the geographic range, with reports indicating a range from 38 to 60 centimeters in some marginal populations, although the 133.2-centimeter value is widely cited for the core Ross Sea stock.

Adult Antarctic toothfish can achieve remarkable dimensions, with the maximum recorded wet weight in the wild reaching 121,000 grams [Wwi = 121,000 grams]. This immense body mass, combined with the ultimate total length of 200 centimeters, places Dissostichus mawsoni among the largest of the Antarctic notothenioids, exceeded only by its congener Dissostichus eleginoides. The weight-length relationship suggests a strongly positive allometric growth pattern, with mass increasing disproportionately as the fish lengthen. Such a large body size is advantageous for a top predator in the deep-sea environment, allowing it to consume sizable prey such as Antarctic silverfish and various squid species. Field surveys and long-term tag-recapture programs have provided robust data on these maximum values, which are critical for setting sustainable catch limits in the managed fishery.

Reproduction in this species occurs at a very low annual rate, consistent with its slow life history. Under the stable thermal regime of the deep Antarctic continental shelf at 1.3 °C [T = 1.3 °C], each mature female produces a single large batch of pelagic eggs per year, with an estimated fecundity of approximately 3,680 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3,680 eggs per spawning event] and a spawning frequency of one event per year [F_R_i = one event per year]. This low annual reproductive output is offset by a long reproductive lifespan and high individual survival, allowing females to contribute offspring over many years. The eggs are large and yolky, providing the developing embryo with sufficient endogenous nutrition to survive the lengthy incubation period. Comparative studies with other nototheniids suggest that this combination of low fecundity and large egg size is an adaptation to the extreme seasonality of primary production in Antarctic waters.

Maximum longevity in Dissostichus mawsoni is considerable, reflecting the low mortality rates typical of deep-sea, cold-water fishes. Tagging studies and otolith age determination have documented individuals reaching an age of approximately 39 years [am = approximately 39 years] in the Ross Sea at the ambient water temperature of 1.3 °C [T = 1.3 °C], making this one of the longer-lived species within the family Nototheniidae. This extended lifespan is thought to be a consequence of the very low metabolic rates enforced by the cold environment, coupled with the absence of significant predation pressure on adults. The slow growth rate, late sexual maturity, and high longevity together form a classic K-selected life-history syndrome that makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing. Management strategies therefore incorporate conservative harvest rates and size limits designed to protect the breeding stock and ensure the long-term persistence of the population. Continued monitoring of age structure is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of these measures.
